## 1. Match structure to signalling mechanism

1. Open [PDB 3SN6](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3SN6), the β₂-adrenergic receptor–Gs complex. Read the method, then open **3D View**. Colour by chain and find the receptor's transmembrane helices and G-protein subunits using the polymer/entity list.
2. Open [PDB 1IEP](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1IEP), the ABL kinase domain bound to **STI-571 (imatinib)**. Select its small-molecule ligand and zoom to the surrounding protein. Read the entry's primary publication summary. This is a **mouse ABL kinase domain**, not the full human BCR–ABL fusion.

**T1.** Where is Gs relative to the receptor's membrane-spanning helices? Why must receptor and G protein contact each other for this signal to pass? `[ELO 3; skill: read a multichain structure]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18, PDB 3SN6)"}
The receptor has **seven transmembrane helices**. Gαs binds its cytoplasmic face, with Gβ and Gγ nearby. Receptor activation promotes GDP release and GTP binding on Gαs, linking extracellular ligand binding to intracellular signalling. The structure also contains experimental stabilising components, including a nanobody; not every chain is part of the native signalling complex.
:::

**T2.** Where does imatinib bind in 1IEP, and why is this a plausible way to inhibit a kinase? `[ELO 3, 9; skill: connect a ligand to a catalytic mechanism]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18, PDB 1IEP)"}
Imatinib occupies the **ATP-binding region and an adjacent pocket** in an inactive ABL kinase conformation. It prevents productive ATP-dependent phosphorylation and stabilises the inactive state. Binding to an isolated domain supports a molecular mechanism; it does not by itself establish clinical efficacy or selectivity against all other kinases.
:::

## 2. Follow a pathway

1. Open [Reactome: signalling by EGFR, R-HSA-177929](https://reactome.org/content/detail/R-HSA-177929).
2. Enter the pathway browser and follow the connection from activated EGFR to RAS and the MAP kinase cascade. Use the molecular details panel to distinguish a protein from a complex or reaction.
3. In your report, draw a short text chain: EGF → EGFR → RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK. Label the receptor, GTPase and kinases. Reactome contains additional branches; this chain is one route.

## 3. Compare target evidence and drug records

1. Open [EGFR in Open Targets](https://platform.opentargets.org/target/ENSG00000146648). In **Associated diseases**, record one cancer association, its evidence types and your access date. Do not assume the highest score proves causation.
2. In **Drugs and clinical candidates**, find one small molecule (for example gefitinib) and one antibody (for example cetuximab). Record the indication and stage rather than writing only “approved”.
3. Open [imatinib in ChEMBL, CHEMBL941](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/explore/compound/CHEMBL941), then **Bioactivities**. Filter for **IC50**, a named target and a binding assay. Inspect the relation symbol, units, assay description and source document. “>100000 nM” is a bound, not an IC50 of 100000 nM.

**T3.** How could a small molecule and an antibody both inhibit EGFR signalling while binding different parts of the receptor? `[ELO 3, 9; skill: interpret drug mechanism records]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18 against EGFR drug records)"}
An ATP-site inhibitor such as **gefitinib** acts on the intracellular kinase domain; **cetuximab** binds the extracellular domain and interferes with receptor activation. Their access, resistance mechanisms and indications differ. Open Targets 26.09 returns **82 drug/candidate records** for EGFR in the provided query, but this changing count is not the number of drugs approved for every EGFR-associated cancer.
:::

**T4. [VG]** Why does imatinib's action on KIT and PDGFRA help explain its use beyond BCR–ABL-driven leukaemia? What evidence would be needed before choosing a drug for a particular tumour? `[ELO 3, 9; skill: compare molecular and clinical evidence]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18 against ChEMBL activity records)"}
Imatinib inhibits **ABL1, KIT and PDGFRA** in many assays. KIT- or PDGFRA-driven gastrointestinal stromal tumours can therefore be sensitive even without BCR–ABL. A target's presence alone is insufficient: the activating variant, drug sensitivity, exposure and clinical evidence for that disease matter. Some variants confer resistance. The R report shows why a pooled activity number cannot settle an individual treatment decision.
:::
